summary: Denmark is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities get 90 days in any 180-day period (ETIAS is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa. Note that the Faroe Islands and Greenland sit outside Schengen and need separate visa endorsements.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

notes: Arriving from outside the EU, the EU's Your Europe portal gives a duty-free allowance of 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer, plus 1 litre of spirits over 22% (or 2 litres of fortified or sparkling wine); 200 cigarettes (or 250 g of tobacco); and other goods worth up to €300, or €430 by air or sea. Under-17s get no alcohol or tobacco allowance.

Between EU countries there is no fixed limit on goods for your own use, but Denmark may set guideline quantities for alcohol and tobacco, which cannot be lower than 800 cigarettes or 10 litres of spirits.
The UK Foreign Office says you cannot take meat, milk or products containing them into the EU, with some exceptions such as powdered baby milk and medically required foods.
The UK Foreign Office says it is illegal to import whale products from Greenland or the Faroe Islands into the UK or EU.

payments.text: No official source we could read describes card acceptance in Denmark. Canada's travel advice says some stores add a surcharge when you pay with a foreign credit card.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office says crime levels are generally low, but pickpockets and bag-snatchers operate in crowded areas, mainly in Copenhagen: the central station, Nørreport Station, Strøget, Christiania, Nyhavn and Kongens Nytorv. It advises extra care in Christiania and Nørrebro, particularly late at night, and says cyclists often have the right of way, so check cycle lanes before turning right.

tips.text: The Faroe Islands and Greenland are not part of the EU or Schengen. A standard Schengen visa is not valid there. If you need a visa, request one specifically endorsed for the Faroes or Greenland when applying.

For most visa-exempt nationals the 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, Greenland and the Faroe Islands combined. The Danish Immigration Service says citizens of Australia, Canada, Chile, Israel, Japan, Malaysia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Korea and the US may stay in Denmark for 90 days or 3 months regardless of earlier stays in other Schengen countries.

The UK Foreign Office and Canada say cyclists often have the right of way in Denmark: drivers should check cycle lanes before turning right, and pedestrians should watch carefully for bicycles when crossing.
ETIAS will cost EUR 20; its official website is travel-europe.europa.eu.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Denmark?
faq.answer: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa, applied for via the nyidanmark.dk portal and the Danish mission serving their residence.

faq.question: Does a Schengen visa cover the Faroe Islands and Greenland?
faq.answer: No. Both territories are part of the Kingdom of Denmark but outside the EU and Schengen. Visa-required travelers need a visa specifically endorsed as valid for the Faroe Islands or Greenland — request this when applying through the Danish authorities.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Denmark?
faq.answer: ETIAS is the EU's travel authorization for visa-exempt visitors. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. Once mandatory, it will cost €20 (free for under-18s and over-70s) and be valid for 3 years.

faq.question: Does Denmark use the euro?
faq.answer: No. Canada's travel advice says the currency of Denmark is the Danish krone (DKK), and that some stores add a surcharge when you pay with a foreign credit card.

faq.question: How do I stay in Denmark longer than 90 days?
faq.answer: Stays over 90 days require a residence permit for a specific purpose — work, study or family — applied for through nyidanmark.dk before travel.
